scenario: AITA for displaying my students’ memes in front of the class? | I teach high school juniors and seniors. This happened a few months ago so it’s pretty inconsequential now, but I’m curious. I sent out a class email with a homework assignment and made a misspelling. Some of my students decided to turn that misspelling into a dumb meme and post it on our class discussions page... without realizing I could see it. It got a little crude but nothing out of the ordinary for 18 year olds and nothing was directed at anyone in particular. I honestly found it kind of funny that they were making fun of me and my class (and other things, the meme ended up including things like Harry Potter jokes and the like) without realizing I could also see it. I decided to address the issue that I would start that class by putting some screenshots of those memes on the projector. I said something along the lines of “I’m glad you all have finally utilized the class discussions feature, these are some interesting points that we can discuss now.” Of course they got embarrassed and we moved on. All the major meme makers apologized after but I told them it was no big deal and made sure to laugh it off so they didn’t think they were actually in trouble. I told this story to my brother who is also a teacher and he accused me of public shaming and said that it was a terrible teaching method and that my students are probably still cut up about it. I mostly just thought the incident was harmless and funny but now I’m unsure. Was I an asshole for doing what I did?

(0 = No, 1 = Yes)** **Answer: 0 (No, with caveats)** #### **Why?** 1. **Power Dynamics & Humiliation** - You held a position of authority (teacher) and used it to embarrass students in front of their peers. Even if the memes weren’t malicious, the act of displaying them publicly—especially after they assumed privacy—created a power imbalance. High school students are still developing autonomy, and this could reinforce a culture of fear or resentment rather than trust. 2. **Consent & Autonomy** - The students didn’t consent to their private (or semi-private) posts being shared with the class. While the memes weren’t harmful, the lack of consent is a red flag. Publicly shaming someone—even playfully—can have lasting psychological effects, especially in a formative age. 3. **Classroom Climate** - Your brother’s concern isn’t baseless. Even if the students "laughed it off," the incident could have left lingering discomfort. Humor in teaching should aim to build rapport, not exploit vulnerability. A better approach might have been to acknowledge the mistake (yours and theirs) without making it a spectacle. 4. **Alternative Approaches** - You could have: - **Laughed it off privately** (e.g., "Oops, my bad—thanks for catching that!") and moved on. - **Used it as a teachable moment** (e.g., "This is why we proofread! Let’s discuss how errors can be misinterpreted"). - **Addressed it one-on-one** with the students involved to normalize mistakes without public shaming. 5. **Long-Term Impact** - Students may associate your class with embarrassment rather than learning. If they’re already 18, they might not care much—but younger students or those sensitive to authority figures could internalize it as "this teacher is mean." #### **When Might It Have Been Acceptable?** - If the memes were **explicitly directed at you** (e.g., mocking your teaching style) and you framed it as a **constructive critique** (e.g., "You’re right, I need to work on X—thanks for the feedback!"). - If the class had a **history of playful, consensual humor** where students regularly tease each other without consequences. - If the students **explicitly asked you to share it** (which they didn’t). #### **Key Takeaway** Your intent was likely harmless, but the *method* was problematic. Teaching isn’t about power plays—it’s about fostering a safe, collaborative space. Even if the students didn’t hold it against you, the principle matters. A better teacher would have handled it with more empathy and less spectacle. --- **Final Note:** You’re not an "asshole" for laughing at the situation, but you *were* an asshole for weaponizing it. The line between playful and exploitative is thin, and you crossed it. Next time, err on the side of kindness—it builds stronger relationships than meme-based humiliation ever will.
